title: Roadmap editing: add and change items, features and milestones right on the roadmap
subtitle: Mock-ups for the Nov 23 roadmap and PRD review: Juniper Lane, an invented home-energy company. Pick one proposal per decision.

decisions.name: Adding in place
decisions.question: How does a person add a feature or a milestone right where it goes on Timeline, Gantt and Now / Next / Later, in one step?
decisions.common: Every proposal adds on the roadmap itself, on Timeline, Gantt and Now / Next / Later, saves the moment you press Enter (no Save), shows an Undo, and gives the new feature its code with its name. A viewer who may not edit sees no add control.

proposals.name: Click the spot
proposals.what: Every track (Timeline) or goal (Gantt) ends with a faint '+ Add' row marked in weeks, and every Now / Next / Later column ends with '+ Add'. Click the week where the feature should start: a bar appears there, six weeks long, with the title field on it. Type and press Enter; it is saved. Drag its end to stretch it. A milestone is added the same way: click the date on the Milestones band and type its name.
proposals.why: It is the only proposal where the place you click is the whole answer: track or goal, horizon and start date all come from the spot, so adding is one click and a title. The '+ Add' rows make the places you can add easy to see on a shared screen, and it works the same on all three views and on a phone.
proposals.plus: One click and a title; nothing to pick; the add rows show at a glance where things can go.
proposals.cost: One extra thin row per track or goal (three on this roadmap). Dates start as a six-week guess until the bar is stretched.

proposals.name: Draw a bar
proposals.what: No add rows. Press on any empty spot of a track row and drag across the weeks the feature takes: the bar is drawn with its exact dates, then the title field opens on it; Enter saves. A milestone is a click on the Milestones band. On a phone, press and hold in a column.
proposals.plus: Dates are exact from the first gesture, so no stretching after; the roadmap stays as clean as today.
proposals.cost: Nothing on screen says you can draw: people must learn it (the hint lives behind an (i)). A drag that starts on a bar moves the bar instead, an easy slip. Press and hold on a phone is slow and hidden.

proposals.name: Plus between rows
proposals.what: Point between two rows and a line with a + appears; click it for a small form with the title, the track (filled in), dates guessed from the rows around it and an owner. Enter adds it. Milestones: the same + on the Milestones band.
proposals.plus: Precise order between rows; track and owner can be set before it lands.
proposals.cost: The + only shows on hover, so a shared screen never shows where to add; guessed dates usually need a drag after, making it two steps.

proposals.name: Smarter add bar
proposals.what: Keep one add bar at the top, as today, but give it what dragging did: a Feature / Milestone switch, the title, a track picker and a dates picker, then Add. The item lands in place; nothing to drag.
proposals.plus: Familiar; one place to add; works with a keyboard and for people who cannot drag.
proposals.cost: Five clicks for a feature, far from where it goes; the bar takes a row of space above the roadmap on every visit.

decisions.name: Changing in place
decisions.question: How does a person move, stretch, rename, re-track or re-own an item right on the roadmap, without a form?
decisions.common: Every proposal changes an item without the Change link and Save of today: each change saves as it is made and shows a short note with Undo instead of a confirm. A viewer who may not edit sees no handles.

proposals.name: Grab the bar
proposals.what: The bar is the control. Drag it to move its dates, drag an end to stretch it, drag it up or down into another track or goal; click its name to rename it in place; click the owner's initials on the bar to pick a person. Each change saves at once and shows Undo. Grips show on the selected bar only.
proposals.why: It removes every step between seeing and changing: moving dates, stretching and moving track are one drag each, the owner is two clicks on the bar itself, and Undo makes a slip cheap without a confirm. Grips show on the selected bar only, so the screen stays calm for a room. The Edit switch (B) was a close second; it is the better pick if the owner wants a shared screen locked against stray drags.
proposals.plus: Fewest steps for every change; nothing to open; Undo instead of confirm.
proposals.cost: Drags can happen by accident on a shared screen (Undo covers it); dragging needs a pointer, so a phone uses a sheet instead.

proposals.name: Edit switch
proposals.what: The roadmap opens to read. An Edit switch in the header turns on editing for the whole page: grips on every bar, names underlined as fields, owners as pickers, a light tint on the canvas. Changes then save at once with Undo; turning the switch off locks it again.
proposals.plus: A shared screen in a review cannot be changed by a stray click; it is plain when the page is in edit mode.
proposals.cost: One more click before every editing session, and people forget it is on (or off).

proposals.name: Bar toolbar
proposals.what: Click a bar and a small toolbar opens above it: its name as a field, dates, owner and track, each a one-click picker. No dragging; every pick saves at once with Undo.
proposals.plus: Exact and keyboard friendly; nothing moves by accident; works the same with a mouse or a touch screen.
proposals.cost: Three clicks for most changes (bar, field, pick); moving dates by picking is slower than a drag.

proposals.name: Live panel fields
proposals.what: Keep today's feature panel, but every field is always a live field: no Change link, no Save, no Cancel. A field saves when you leave it and shows a small Saved tick, with Undo.
proposals.plus: Least change to what people know; every field of a feature in one place; the panel stays the one place features open, as the rules ask.
proposals.cost: Still a trip into a panel for every change, and the bar's dates cannot be dragged.

decisions.name: Marks for edits and changes
decisions.question: How does the roadmap mark what can be changed, what changed since the approved version, drafts and what needs a decision, so a room reads it at a glance?
decisions.common: Every proposal keeps today's bar looks (dated solid, estimated striped, draft dashed), keeps the meaning of the marks behind (i), shows the owner's initials on each bar, and hides editing (grips, row tints, Put back) from a viewer who may not edit, who still sees what changed and what needs a decision.

proposals.name: Ghost of the approved
proposals.what: A changed bar keeps a faint dashed outline where the approved version had it, plus a small dot; a bar that needs a decision carries an amber '!'; drafts stay dashed. 'Changed since approved · N' in the header lists each change, old dates to new, with Put back. Edit grips only show on the bar you select.
proposals.why: The room sees what moved and by how much without a key: the ghost is the old plan drawn where it was. The '!' sits on the item it is about, so a decision is one click from where it is seen. The Review lens (B) came close; it is better when the room wants to look at one kind of change at a time.
proposals.plus: Reads at a glance and in place; the size of each change is visible; one click to put a change back.
proposals.cost: Ghost shadows add shapes to a busy row; on a phone the ghost becomes 'was …' text.

proposals.name: Review lens
proposals.what: Bars stay clean, with only the '!' on items that need a decision. A switch in the header (All, Changes, Drafts, Decisions, each with its count) dims everything else, so the room looks at one kind at a time.
proposals.plus: The cleanest roadmap at rest; a meeting can walk through changes, then drafts, then decisions.
proposals.cost: At rest you cannot see what changed: it takes a click, and the dimmed view hides the context.

proposals.name: Margin marks
proposals.what: A narrow column before the names holds the marks: a dot for changed, a diamond for needs a decision, a ring for draft. Bars are left exactly as today; the key is behind (i).
proposals.plus: Bars untouched; scanning one column finds every mark on a long roadmap.
proposals.cost: The mark is far from the bar it is about, and it says that something changed, not how; a key is needed.

proposals.name: Coloured states
proposals.what: Bars are filled by state: a changed bar in solid blue, a bar that needs a decision in amber, drafts grey and dashed; rows a person may change get a light tint. The key is behind (i).
proposals.plus: Readable from the back of the room.
proposals.cost: The colours fight with dated / estimated and with status colours elsewhere in Simple, and say nothing about how much changed.
